source: Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994) Exploring the planning fallacy, Study 1 (honors thesis)
finding: Students near the end of an honors thesis gave a best-guess finish time, an 'everything goes well' time and an 'everything goes badly' time. All three were too early on average. Best guesses still tracked the real order of finish times.
numbers: N=37 Waterloo psychology students (32 usable; 4 never finished by the cut-off). Best guess 33.9 days vs actual 55.5, t(32)=3.43, p<.002; only 29.7% finished by their best guess. Optimistic scenario 27.4 days (10.8% on time). Pessimistic scenario 48.6 days, still under the 55.5 actual. Correlation of best guess with actual r=.77.
limits: One cohort of students, one task. Shows the inside view is optimistic. Does not test a class lookup. Gap 10 answered for this founding lab study only.
agent_relevance: Asking for a worst case is not a substitute for a class lookup: the stated worst case was still 7 days too early. An S0 step should pull a class distribution, not ask the model to imagine a bad scenario.

source: Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994) Study 4 (recall and recall-relevant conditions)
finding: Students predicted when they would finish a computer assignment. Simply recalling past similar assignments did not fix optimism. Recalling them AND being asked to link them to this task (give the usual finish time, write a scenario that ends at that usual time) removed the bias in the mean. But absolute accuracy did not improve, and the recalled past times were later than the real time on this task.
numbers: N=123 students, 3 thought-focus conditions x 2 deadlines. Mean predicted vs actual days: control 5.5 vs 6.8; recall 5.3 vs 6.3; recall-relevant 7.0 vs 7.0. Finished by predicted time: 29.3% control, 38.1% recall, 60.0% recall-relevant, chi2(2)=7.63, p<.01. ANOVA on absolute error: no effect of thought focus. Even in recall-relevant, very few mentioned the past in think-aloud.
limits: Authors say they lack compelling evidence that recalling one's own past improves accuracy; relying on the recalled times would have made estimates too pessimistic. Personal class, not an external class.
agent_relevance: Having class facts in context is not enough; the step must force a link from class to case (a stated class estimate that the final answer must be anchored on). Supports 'class number first, then adjust', and warns that a class can be mismatched to the case.

source: Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994) Study 5 (observers predicting another person)
finding: Observers yoked to Study 4 control participants were given the actor's thoughts, the actor's past completion times, or both. Observers used the past far more than the actors did, and their predictions were later than both the actors' predictions and the real finish times.
numbers: N=123 observers. Spontaneously mentioned the actor's past: 48.0% of observers vs 2.4% of actors (chi2(1,N=164)=48.78); 73.2% (memories) and 65.9% (both) vs 4.8% (thoughts only). Observer predictions ran about 8.0 to 8.8 days vs the actors' 5.5 predicted and 6.8 actual (table columns are garbled in the extracted text, so the per-condition split is uncertain).
limits: Observers over-corrected because the actors' recalled past times were longer than what happened. Supports 'class use is easy for an outsider, hard for the planner'. Gives no rule for how much to trust the class.
agent_relevance: The agent is the outsider on user cases. Third-person framing of the user's case ('a project like this') may help trigger class use. Also: over-reliance on a pessimistic class is a real error mode.

source: Flyvbjerg (2003) Delusions of Success: Comment on Dan Lovallo and Daniel Kahneman, Harvard Business Review, December
finding: Reply to Lovallo and Kahneman 2003. Argues their cure (outside view) works only if the forecaster is a victim of honest optimism. If forecasts are deliberately cooked under organisational pressure, there is little incentive to accept the outside view. Cites 70 years of transport data with the same error size and frequency, so no learning.
numbers: Urban rail cost overruns about 45% in constant prices; patronage about 50% below forecast. Four explanations tested (technical, economic, psychological, political); political fits best. No sample size in this short comment.
quote: Lovallo and Kahneman's analysis of the planning fallacy seems valid mainly where political pressures are insignificant.
limits: This is the commentary on the founding article, not the founding article. The 2003 Lovallo and Kahneman HBR text was not obtainable. Gap 10 stays open for that article (N, design, effect unknown to us; it is a practitioner article).
agent_relevance: When the user's own prompt pushes a rosy number (a pitch, a plan to defend), the class lookup is the part most likely to be overridden. S0 output should be written before the user's preferred answer is considered.

source: Lovallo, Clarke and Camerer (2012) Robust analogizing and the outside view: two empirical tests of case-based decision making, Strategic Management Journal 33(5)
finding: Abstract only (from Crossref and OpenAlex records; full text is closed and the Caltech copy returned 403). Test 1, private-equity investment decisions: an outside view built from a reference class of analogies beat a few analogies the decision maker already knew. Test 2, film revenue: similarity-based forecasting, which blends reference class forecasting with case-based reasoning, beat regression models.
numbers: No numbers obtained. Sample sizes and effect sizes unknown to us.
limits: Not opened. Closest peer-reviewed field test of 'many analogies beat few familiar ones', which bears on gap 3 (how to combine classes), but we cannot cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Suggests weighting by similarity over a broad set rather than choosing one class. Candidate rule to test: similarity-weighted average over several classes. Not verified.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers and Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment, JDM 11(5): training, practice and CHAMPS KNOW tags (re-read for unit, ANOVA and design)
finding: The score is a Brier score standardized within each question (deviation from that question's mean), so it removes question difficulty by construction. Tags come from forecasters ticking boxes on their own explanations. The training manipulation was randomized, but the tag analysis is correlational and the authors say it would be going too far to credit only comparison classes.
numbers: Table 5 means: comparison classes 0.17 (n=580), math/stat models 0.26 (453), select questions 0.26 (330), hunt for information 0.38 (2,992), update 0.44, post-mortem 1.04, control 0.49 (6,622), categorized 0.42 (4,627), uncategorized 0.37 (2,087). Table 6 ANOVA (1 df): comparison classes F=12.28, p<.001; post-mortem F=9.38, p=.002; only C, P and O significant. Forecasts per subject similar across arms (year 1: 86.76 no training vs 84.29 probability training).
limits: All 'standardized' means are positive, which plain deviation-from-mean would not give; the exact transform is not stated, so only rank order is safe. The 'SD' column (0.003) looks like an SE. Tag is self-selected, so skilled forecasters may pick it. Gap 5 partly closed: difficulty is controlled by construction, the unit is still undefined, and no randomized test of the outside-view instruction alone exists.
agent_relevance: Do not quote 0.17 vs 0.26 as an effect size. The honest reading is 'comparison-class users were more accurate than users of other tags, on the same questions, not randomized'.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott and Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Randomized test with human forecasters. One GPT-4-Turbo assistant was told to start by identifying reference classes and base rates (superforecasting prompt). Another was told to neglect base rates and be overconfident (noisy). Both beat a weaker control assistant. The base-rate-neglecting assistant was almost as helpful as the good one.
numbers: N=991 humans, 6 questions, 3 conditions. Mean error: control 0.89, superforecasting 0.68, noisy 0.64. Both treatments vs control p<.001 (diffs -0.21 and -0.25). Superforecasting vs noisy: diff 0.04, p=.391. Without question 3: 0.40 vs 0.47 vs control 0.67; superforecasting vs noisy p=.024. Abstract: accuracy gains 24 to 28%, or 41% vs 29% without the outlier.
limits: Human users, not an autonomous agent. The assistant gave numeric forecasts to humans, so the gain may come from any numeric anchor. Only 6 questions. The prompt bundles base rates with the ten commandments.
agent_relevance: Warning: a visible numeric anchor helps even when it comes from a base-rate-neglecting model, so an S0 gain measured against a no-number control may be an anchoring effect, not a class effect. The right control for an S0 test is an arm with a plausible but class-free number.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock and Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities, Study 2 (six models incl. o1 and o1-mini)
finding: Study 2 added reasoning models (o1, o1-mini) to Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Llama 3.1 405B and ran compound and adapted prompts on the same 100 questions. No prompt helped in the preregistered mixed model, base-rate prompts included. All models scored about the same.
numbers: Mean Brier by model: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 3.1 405B 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.207. Mixed-model estimates vs control (Table 8): Base Rate First + Frequency-Based -0.004 (adj p=.985); Base Rate First + Chain of Thought 0.000 (adj p=.985); Mandatory Probability + Base Rate Fallback +0.006 (adj p=.985). Superforecaster-authored Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt worse: +0.023, adj p=.01. About 19,000 forecasts targeted per model; refusals cut some models' counts.
limits: No per-model interaction was reported for base-rate prompts, so gap 4 gets only indirect evidence: the reasoning models were not better and base-rate prompts did not help any model on average. Model knowledge cut-offs in 2023 to 2024.
agent_relevance: No sign that a base-rate prompt helps weak models more than reasoning models, or the reverse; the average effect is near zero for all six. Do not expect S0 wording to move Brier by more than a few thousandths on frontier models.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han and Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models (re-read for prompt order, hedging and ensembling)
finding: In the Halawi prompt the base-rate check is the LAST step: write arguments for and against, weigh them, then check for over- or under-confidence and consider historical base rates. The system hedged away from extremes and lost to the crowd where the crowd was confident.
numbers: Crowd within .3-.7: system Brier .199 vs crowd .246. Crowd within .05 of 0 or 1: system accuracy +7% but Brier worse by .04. Example: crowd 1%, system 20% (Kevin McCarthy question, resolved NO), although the output mentions base rates. Ensembling on validation: trimmed mean .1649, median .1651, mean .1656, geometric mean .1655, no ensemble .1676, USC .1691, human crowd .1600.
limits: Fine-tuned GPT-4 with safety-trained hedging; later models may hedge less. Base-rate step never ablated or moved. Gap 1 stays open here (late placement is the only placement tested); gap 6 gets suggestive evidence.
agent_relevance: A late base-rate check does not stop a model drifting to 20% when the class says 1%. Test S0 as a floor/ceiling: if the class rate is below 5% or above 95%, the final answer needs an explicit reason to leave that band.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen et al. (2024) Reasoning and tools for human-level forecasting: system prompt principles, sample trace and ensemble spread
finding: The system prompt lists forecasting principles, including 'don't ignore base rates' and 'approximate the same quantity several ways, then combine with a weighted or trimmed mean or median'. In the printed trace the agent asks 'Do I need a tool?', recalls a base rate from memory ('assuming a 30% chance'), then averages 30%, 35%, 40% into 35%.
numbers: 201 Manifold questions. RTF ReAct ensemble of 3: median Brier .169, mean .170, one sampled run .180, crowd .172. Ensemble standard deviation 0.092 for ReAct agents (size 3) vs 0.150 for base LMs (size 4). Base LMs: ensembling did not help (0.218 vs 0.210 for GPT-4o). Halawi GPT-4o baseline .177.
limits: No ablation of the base-rate principle. The '30% vs 8%' spread quoted earlier is not in this text; the measured spread is the ensemble SD above. The combination rule (plain average of base-rate, news and model estimates) is used but never compared with alternatives.
agent_relevance: Shows the failure to avoid: a recalled class number with no tool lookup, then an equal-weight average that dilutes it. Gap 3: the only combination rule in use is a plain average, untested against picking the best class.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino and Morris (2024) Can language models use forecasting strategies? (re-read for the base-rate pipeline)
finding: The Base Rates strategy is a two-call pipeline: the model first writes a question about how often similar events happened, then answers it from its own memory, then forecasts with that sentence in the prompt. No search, no data. It produced the worst weighted Brier.
numbers: Validation Brier: Human .1334, Basic .1221, Base Rates .1562, Both Sides .1553. Weighted (Yes and No outcomes averaged equally): Human .1746, Base Rates .2540 (worst), Crowd .1860. Base Rates scored about .4545 on events that resolved Yes vs about .0534 on No (reconstructed from the weighted table; rows are ambiguously labeled in the extraction). Most events resolve No.
limits: PaLM 2, events resolving mostly in 2022. Recalled, not retrieved or computed, base rates. Answers gap 2 from the 'recalled' side only.
agent_relevance: A model-recalled class frequency can drag probabilities down and hurt on events that happen. If recalled, label the number 'recalled, unverified' and keep the interval wide.

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic forecasting with structured linguistic beliefs (BLF): empirical priors
finding: On ForecastBench dataset questions, the base rate per source and question subtype, computed by counting past resolutions, is a strong baseline, and the search agent adds only a little on top. Giving the same prior to the agent changes little for it, but helps a no-LLM baseline.
numbers: Brier Index (higher is better; 50 = always 0.5): empirical-prior baseline 58.3 on dataset questions, full BLF 62.7; crowd+prior baseline 69.9 overall; BLF paired gain +3.4 overall, +4.5 on data (significant), +2.3 ns on market questions. Priors by subtype: ACLED 10x spike 0.00, Wikipedia vaccine 0.00, FIDE Elo 1% 0.01, swimming WR 0.99, ACLED any increase 0.23. 400 question-date instances.
quote: The empirical prior has negligible effect on BLF (which acquires better data via search), but helps the no-LLM baseline.
limits: Counted priors use all data before each question. Not randomized across question types. The agent already searches, which may cover the class lookup. Gap 2 largely answered: computed class frequencies are strong, and the LLM's edge over them is small (+4.5 BI points on data).
agent_relevance: Supports tool-side class counting: when a data source exists, compute the frequency and give it to the agent; expect the agent to add only a few points beyond it.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF, Appendix G.1: KNN class frequency for DBnomics (computed class rate, no LLM)
finding: For seasonal weather questions the system bypasses the LLM with a code-computed class frequency: count past values within 10 days of the same day of year (about 270 neighbours from 14 years) that exceeded the threshold, with Laplace smoothing. Feeding the series straight to the LLM was reported as worse than this counter.
numbers: Brier Index on 40 questions (119 resolution dates): KNN 59.1, always-0.5 baseline 50.0, Cassi reference 51.0. Formula: (count above threshold + 1) / (neighbours + 2).
limits: Small n (40 questions), one source family. The LLM-on-raw-series row is described in words but was not tabulated in the extracted text. Gap 8 (code-side arithmetic) answered in direction only.
agent_relevance: Template for the arithmetic operator: count in code, smooth, hand the number to the model. The model should choose the class and window, not do the counting.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF: trial averaging and shrinkage selection
finding: The authors built a shrinkage rule that pulls the averaged forecast toward the prior (crowd or empirical) when trial-to-trial dispersion is high, tuned by leave-one-out cross-validation. Without crowd or prior anchors, the tuning chose no shrinkage (equal to plain logit averaging).
numbers: Without anchors, 400 ForecastBench questions, 791 events: arithmetic mean gains with more trials K (1 to 5), a small extra gain from the logit mean, LOO shrinkage coincides with logit averaging (f=1, c=0). Default K=5 trials.
limits: This is shrinkage driven by disagreement between runs, not by the class rate being extreme. Anchors were off in this analysis, so it does not test 'move toward the class rate'. Gap 6 stays open.
agent_relevance: Once runs are averaged in logit space, a pull toward the prior was not worth it. Averaging several independent runs may capture part of what a class pull would give.

source: Ye, Dineen et al. (2026) Hindcast: replaying prediction markets to evaluate LLM forecasters
finding: Retrieval agents with a first-step 'prior anchor' (five fixed probability bands by question type) improved Brier on 8 of 9 open models, but hurt on Entertainment: nearly all 'will X be #1 on Billboard' questions resolve No, a model with no retrieval sits near that base rate and is right, and the agent reads fan hype as evidence for Yes and argues itself out of the right default.
numbers: 216 markets; 83% of the resolved pool is NO (2,851 of 3,427). Brier up to 23% lower with retrieval (Qwen3-32B .234 to .179). Net recoveries minus regressions by topic: Entertainment -31, Other -10, Elections/politics -7, Social/celebrity -7, Tech/AI -5. Per model: Qwen3-8B +43; R1-Distill-Qwen-7B -19 (accuracy and Brier both worse, attributed to long reasoning chains crowding out evidence).
limits: Small open models (3B to 32B), Reddit corpus. The prior-anchor step is in every agent run and was not ablated. The one small reasoning model was hurt by the scaffold, which is only indirect evidence for gap 4.
agent_relevance: When the class says 'almost always No', an evidence-gathering step can wreck it. S0 should output a stated floor or ceiling, and the evidence step should have to beat it with a stated reason, not a tally of favourable items.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR): scratchpad prompt with reference-class step
finding: The benchmark's scratchpad prompt (taken from Halawi) puts a reference class and base rate as step 2, straight after rephrasing the question. So the scratchpad baseline is an S0-early scaffold bundled with 7 other steps. It beat zero-shot for some models and by little for others.
numbers: Table 19, 1,000-question LLM set, no extra information: GPT-4o scratchpad .147 (dataset .194, market .100) vs zero-shot .168 (.211, .124); Gemini-1.5-Pro scratchpad .143 vs zero-shot .147. Superforecasters .076 vs GPT-4o .130 on combination plus standard questions: gap 0.054, vs 0.026 between GPT-4o and GPT-4 (confirms the earlier b17 line). The table text is messy, so other model rows were not used.
limits: Bundle, not ablation. Paired rows were read by hand from a garbled PDF table. Dataset-type questions drive the difference.
agent_relevance: Another bundle result: S0-early plus 7 other steps improved GPT-4o by 0.021 and Gemini by 0.004 over a direct answer. Still no isolated S0 measure (gap 1 stays open).

source: Becker, Rush, Barnes and Rein (2025, METR) Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developer productivity
finding: Randomized trial with a planning-fallacy flavour: developers and experts predicted that AI tools would cut task time, and the measured result went the other way. Developers kept believing in a speedup after the study. Neither group used a class of earlier AI productivity studies.
numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks (about 2.0 hours each). Developers forecast 24% less time with AI before; estimated 20% less after; measured 19% MORE time. Economists predicted 39% shorter, ML experts 38% shorter. Correlation of per-task forecast time with actual time 0.64 (AI allowed) and 0.59 (disallowed).
limits: Small sample (16 people), early-2025 tools, experienced contributors on familiar repositories. A direction-of-effect result, not a test of outside-view prompts.
agent_relevance: Domain example for gap 9: in software effort tasks the class is a set of earlier time-tracking studies, and the experts' inside views failed. People's per-task time forecasts were informative (r about .6) while their view of the tool effect was biased.

source: Araya (2025) Do chains-of-thought of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases or phobias in Bayesian reasoning?
finding: Three reasoning LLMs solved one hidden-card Bayesian puzzle. Without any hint all three used symbolic Bayes and none used natural frequencies. When told to use Gigerenzer's natural frequencies, they used them inconsistently, often mixing back to percentages; one chain ran for thousands of words.
numbers: Gemini Flash 2.0, o3-mini, DeepSeek R1 (Feb 2025); one problem. Gemini correct in 255 words in one run and wrong in 389 in another; o3-mini wrong in the first run (2,039 words); DeepSeek R1 chains 5,504 to 8,457 words. No statistics.
limits: One problem, three models, qualitative. Not a forecasting test. Answers gap 8 only as 'LLMs do not spontaneously use frequency formats and follow the instruction unevenly'.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the model to count in natural frequencies in text. Put the counting in code, or give it the counts already as 'N out of M'.

source: Huang, Fayek and Zhang (2025) REFER: mitigating bias in opinion summarisation via frequency framed prompting
finding: Prompting the model to first count how often each opinion appears (an explicit reference class) before summarising improved fairness for larger models but did little for small ones: Llama 3-8B skipped the counting step and went straight to a qualitative summary, while Llama 3-70B counted first. An oracle prompt with the true counts served as an upper bound.
numbers: Fairness metrics over FairSumm tweets and Amazon reviews; exact deltas not parsed. Result stated by the authors as 'reduced effectiveness' with Llama 3-8B and 'strong performance' with larger models.
limits: Summarisation fairness, not forecasting. Included as the only 2025 study found that tests a count-first frequency step across model sizes (gap 4 and 8, indirect).
agent_relevance: A class-first or count-first instruction needs a model that can follow a multi-part order. Weak models may silently skip S0; check the output for the class number and do not proceed without it.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping and Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters: Brier and base rates
finding: Brier scores are not comparable across question sets with different base rates. A forecaster who always states the true base rate b gets expected Brier b(1-b). Perfectly predicting rare events barely moves a mixed-set average, while a small gain on coin-flip questions moves it a lot. Calibration alone can reward a constant base-rate forecaster.
numbers: Example: 50 questions at 50% base rate plus 50 at 5%. Perfect on the rare ones (0.0475 to 0) and baseline elsewhere gives 0.125 total; clueless on rare ones but 0.25 to 0.15 on coin flips gives about 0.1. A constant 1% forecaster on 100 cardinals is perfectly calibrated. Our own arithmetic: at a 5% class rate, answering 20% costs 0.070 vs 0.0475 expected Brier.
limits: Argument and worked examples, not an empirical test of S0.
agent_relevance: Any S0 experiment must stratify by class rate or use a skill score against the per-class base-rate forecaster; otherwise the dataset's Yes rate decides the winner.
